rationale: The incumbent edition carried a migration-era assessment with no steelman, no components, no research priority, and no per-claim treatments, so it could not be re-adopted as it stood: every featured claim must have a complete treatment. The ledger has also moved since that edition. Four new evidence records enter from Peripato et al. 2023 — a basin-wide earthwork comparator (AMZ-E038, AMZ-E039, logged as context for AMZ-C004) and a tree-species corroboration of AMZ-C008 (AMZ-E040, AMZ-E041) that the verifier flags as non-independent of Levis 2017 — together with two new claims (AMZ-C029, AMZ-C033) and a new research item (AMZ-R006). None of this changes the case verdict: the heterogeneous-Amazon reading remains well_supported from both directions, and Carvajal's qualitative credibility remains provisionally_supported pending the corridor test. What changes is the treatment layer. AMZ-C004 is still established as a statement of what the 2026 study documents and predicts, but its diagnosticity summary now records that published earthwork totals differ several-fold between models (the 2026 regional projection exceeds the 2023 basin-wide upper bound) and that only a promise-blind stratified survey can calibrate them. AMZ-C008 records that the new corroboration comes from inside one research network and is subject to the same post-Columbian confound, so it counts once. The featured set grows from twenty to twenty-five by adding the rungs on which the sparse-Amazon account stands or falls — AMZ-C020 (site-type proportions), AMZ-C021 (the thinness of the negative sampling), AMZ-C022 (time-graded erasure of the signal), AMZ-C029 (the basin-wide low-probability fraction, graded unresolved because its intended evidence record failed quote verification) — and the collapse mechanism AMZ-C023, all of which the incumbent article already leaned on without featuring. AMZ-C024, AMZ-C025 and AMZ-C033 stay catalogued as supporting detail under their parents but remain spanned in the article. Load-bearing now names AMZ-C003 explicitly, since AMZ-E007 is the single record whose removal most changes the Carvajal leg, and AMZ-C014 as the second leg of the matrix half. The steelman is written for the first time. The article adds an explicit side-by-side of five accounts with their predictions, a section on what would decide among them keyed to the six research items, the earthwork-model comparator and its incommensurability caveats, the geographic caution that the dated contact-horizon settlement systems lie off Carvajal's most famous reaches, and honest flags on the claims that rest on a verified source anchor without a separate evidence record. AMZ-R006 joins the crux order after the corridor test, the witness table and the promise-blind surveys. All four plates are retained in their sections. The question is unchanged; the accounts are stated for the first time.
accounts: Invention: Carvajal fabricated or grossly inflated a riverine world the Amazon could never have supported
A murdered world: Carvajal described faithfully what he saw, and epidemics, slave raids, missionization and flight destroyed and dispersed it before later travelers arrived
The garden Amazon: the whole basin, interfluves included, was densely peopled and intensively managed by many millions
The mosaic: dense, engineered corridors and hotspots set in a lightly occupied forest matrix, with Carvajal qualitatively honest and numerically unreliable

The modest skeptic: real but modest societies on the richest corridors, population totals that are model artefacts, and a later emptiness that partly records a modest reality rather than only a collapse
article:
In the summer of 1542, a starving Dominican friar floated down a river no European had ever descended, keeping notes. Gaspar de Carvajal was the chaplain of Francisco de Orellana's accidental expedition — fifty-odd men in a makeshift brigantine who had set out to find cinnamon and ended up crossing South America by water. What he recorded was not wilderness. [His chronicle describes populous riverbank settlements running for leagues, storehouses of food, travelled roads leading inland, fine ceramics, and organized polities — alternating with stretches he reports as empty]{claim=AMZ-C001}.

For most of the twentieth century, educated opinion held that he was lying, or at best embellishing. The Amazon of the textbooks was a “counterfeit paradise”: soils too poor, protein too scarce, floods too brutal for anything beyond small shifting villages. An eyewitness account of crowded riverbanks was an embarrassment to be explained away — a friar magnifying marvels for patrons back home. And later travelers, arriving a century and more afterward, found mostly what the textbooks predicted: forest, and silence.

This case is about what happens when the instruments catch up with the argument — and about the discipline required to say precisely how much of the friar's world they have found.

## Five ways to read the friar

Set the serious readings side by side, because the evidence below sorts among them unevenly.

- **Invention.** Carvajal made up or grossly inflated a world that never existed; the Amazon could not have supported it. This predicts no large contact-era settlements along his route and no independent witnesses to them.
- **A murdered world.** Carvajal described faithfully what he saw; epidemics, slave raids, missions, and flight destroyed and scattered it before the next visitors arrived. This predicts dense contact-horizon archaeology in his populated reaches and documented collapse mechanisms operating specifically on riverbanks.
- **The garden Amazon.** The whole basin — interfluves included — was densely peopled and intensively managed, by many millions. This predicts intensive-use signals nearly everywhere the soils are cored.
- **The mosaic.** Dense, engineered corridors and hotspots set in a lightly occupied forest matrix; Carvajal is qualitatively honest and numerically unreliable. This predicts strong signals near rivers and bluffs and weak ones in the deep interfluves.
- **The modest skeptic.** Real societies, but smaller than the eyewitnesses imply; Orellana travelled the richest corridors, archaeology looks where it can see, and the emptier later Amazon partly records a modest reality rather than only a collapse. This predicts that population models fall apart under their own assumptions and that the negative record holds up under better sampling.

The first reading has not survived. The other four are live, and the question of proportion — how much corridor, how much matrix — is what separates them.

## The account, and its two texts

Before weighing Carvajal against archaeology, there is a problem inside the text itself. His chronicle survives in two main manuscript families, and they do not say the same things. [The most famous numbers — 50,000 warriors, 10,000, 8,000, villages four and five leagues long — appear in the Medina/Muñoz branch but not in Oviedo's version, which preserves the same crowded world with one figure of about 5,000 warriors]{claim=AMZ-C002}. Whatever else is true, the extreme figures are textually unstable in a way the qualitative picture is not. A serious reading of Carvajal was never “believe him” or “dismiss him”; it is: trust the kind of world he described, refuse his arithmetic. Which figure sits in which witness is exactly the sort of detail that deserves a passage-by-passage collation, and this record does not yet hold one; the branch comparison it relies on is a geographer's, verified from a scanned copy.

And his description does not stand alone. [A Portuguese soldier, Diogo Nunes, had entered the same Machiparo province four years before Orellana, and the ten surviving accounts of the 1560 Ursúa expedition independently describe dense settlement, maize stores one chronicler called infinite, long straight roads “in the manner of the Incas of Peru, except for the walls,” and ceramics of famous quality]{claim=AMZ-C003} — on the same reaches, from witnesses who were not copying one another and mostly detested each other. None of them repeats Carvajal's giant numbers. All of them repeat his world. Two limits travel with this: fortifications and organized warfare are not among the features the witnesses share, and the exact tributaries of the route are still argued — [one river in Carvajal's itinerary is glossed in the scholarship with an explicit question mark]{claim=AMZ-C024}.

## What the lasers found

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P01}

The modern turn begins when researchers notice geometric ditches emerging from deforested pasture in the Brazilian state of Acre — and accelerates when LiDAR, which strips the canopy off the terrain model, goes looking under the trees. The survey program led by Martti Pärssinen and Alceu Ranzi has published its reckoning: [flying 4,430 kilometers of laser lines, it documented 432 earthworks where satellite imagery had found a fraction of that, and projects roughly 24,000 to 30,000 monuments across a 183,000-square-kilometer cultural region]{claim=AMZ-C004} — as many earthworks in one corner of the basin as had once been guessed for all of Amazonia.

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P02}

Three honesty notes belong here, and this site is built to make them. First: the study proposes a peak population of 1.25 to 3 million people — but [that figure is an assumption engine, resting on how many earthworks were in use at once and on about 300 people per monument, and the paper's own alternative reading of the same data yields roughly 250,000 to 600,000]{claim=AMZ-C005}. The monuments are certain; the census is a model. Second, and larger: the Aquiry florescence is dated to roughly AD 100–300. It is decisive evidence that Amazonian environments could carry monument-building societies — and weak evidence about what Orellana saw fourteen centuries later. This case refuses to spend ancient grandeur as contact-era corroboration. Third: the regional projection sits beside a basin-wide one that does not obviously agree with it. A 2023 predictive model, built from earthworks known before this LiDAR campaign, estimates 10,272 to 23,648 undiscovered earthworks across all 6.7 million square kilometers of Amazonia, and places nearly all of its highest-probability cells in a 94,713-square-kilometer rectangle over Acre. The 2026 study projects more than that model's basin-wide upper bound within one region roughly twice the size of that rectangle. The two are not strictly commensurable — different definitions of “earthwork,” different data, different estimators — so the comparison does not contradict what the 2026 study says it predicts. It does show that published earthwork totals differ several-fold between models, and that only a survey chosen blind to promise, stratified by predicted probability, can tell which is calibrated.

**Transparency.** The 2026 study's funding statement reads, in its own words: “The project and data collection were funded by a grant from E. Jhong (USA).” That is this site's founder. The Athanatos Foundation, with which he is associated, is acknowledged for administrative assistance. Readers should know this — and should notice that it is exactly why this case presents the paper's population claim at its most assumption-exposed, not its most headline-friendly.

What matters for Carvajal is the archaeology whose dates overlap him. [An 1,800-kilometer arc of the southern rim was occupied by earth-building societies in fortified villages around AD 1250–1500]{claim=AMZ-C006}, with its own population model — half a million to a million — stated as a model that depends on every site being lived in at once. And [several major settlement systems ran into the contact era and beyond: the Belterra Plateau towns near Santarém from about AD 1300 to seventeenth-century colonization, complete with dark earths, ponds, and trodden roads; Marajó's Cacoal site to 1650; and Upper Xingu settlements inhabited until about 1770, their plaza-and-road layouts matching the villages living Kuikuro communities build today]{claim=AMZ-C011}. That last point deserves its own sentence: some of this is not a lost world at all, but a continuous one — collapsed in numbers, unbroken in pattern. The caution is geographic: Santarém, Marajó, and the Xingu are the lower Amazon and its southern tributaries, not the Machiparo and Omagua reaches where Carvajal's most famous passages sit.

## Engineered ground

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P03}

The subsistence question — *what could they all have eaten?* — was always the strongest scientific objection, and it now has at least one direct answer. [In the Llanos de Mojos, the Casarabe culture ran intensive year-round maize agriculture on a savannah it had replumbed: drainage canals for the wet season, farm ponds for the dry, documented by phytoliths in the fields themselves]{claim=AMZ-C007}. More broadly, [dark earths, raised-field complexes, forest islands, and orchard-like concentrations of domesticated trees around archaeological sites record long human engineering of Amazonian ground]{claim=AMZ-C008}.

{plate:IMG-AMZ-P04}

The savannah's waters were engineered too, and this deserves a moment, because “they couldn't have gotten enough protein” was for decades the respectable core of the impossibility argument. [Zigzag weirs and straight causeways cross the Llanos de Mojos floodplains, and most of the hundreds of detected ponds sit within thirty-five meters of one — V-shaped structures built to concentrate fish as the floods receded]{claim=AMZ-C019}. And the diet is in the ground, not just the infrastructure: [one settlement's refuse holds more than seventeen thousand fish bones, including dry-season species like lungfish that persist in small waters — year-round aquatic harvest, fifty kilometers from the big river]{claim=AMZ-C026}. Honest limits travel with both: the weir study itself notes these structures concentrate fish far less intensely than modern analogues elsewhere, and one site's refuse is an existence proof, not a census. But the specific claim the old skepticism rested on — that the interfluves could not feed sedentary people through the year — now has documented counterexamples in both engineering and bone. Note also the calendar: the Casarabe world ends around 1400, a century and a half before Orellana. It answers the impossibility argument; it does not describe 1542.

Engineering is not a census, and this case keeps the distinction structural. [The raised fields of the Bolivian lowlands, dated carefully, show intermittent construction and use — plausibly flood-risk works built where nothing else would do — not a permanent breadbasket]{claim=AMZ-C009}. And the domesticated-forest signal carries a first-class qualifier: five post-Columbian centuries have shaped the modern forest too, and the formal critique arguing they did most of the shaping is part of this record, not a footnote to it. A second study finds that [across 1,676 forest plots, 53 of 79 domesticated tree species track the modelled probability that earthworks are present]{claim=AMZ-C033} — corroboration, but from inside the same research network, using the same species list, and open to the same post-Columbian confound. The record counts it once, not twice.

## How many people?

The honest answer to the famous question is that the published numbers — one million, five, six, ten — are not competing measurements. They are competing models, and several descend from the same assumptions. The field's most influential estimator said so himself: [Denevan publicly rejected the habitat-density method behind his own 5.1–6.8 million figure, while still judging “at least 5 to 6 million” reasonable on other grounds]{claim=AMZ-C012}. A number can outlive the death of the argument that produced it; a reader deserves to know when that has happened.

What the aggregate evidence does support: [radiocarbon proxies for the whole biome fit a population growing logistically toward carrying capacity right up to European arrival]{claim=AMZ-C015} — no sign, at basin scale, that Amazonian societies were already dying out on their own before the caravels. The authors' own caveats govern: the proxy tracks relative change, its terminal dip is attributed to sampling bias compounded by post-contact collapse, and “carrying capacity (however high)” says nothing about how high.

## The disappearance

If Carvajal described a real world, where did it go? The documented answer, where colonial records permit counting, is brutal and specific. [In the Napo–Aguarico province, an estimated 49,000–51,000 people in the early contact period became about 6,000 by 1700 — an 88 percent collapse; neighboring Mainas lost roughly two-thirds — through differing regional mixtures of epidemics, slave raids, missionization, forced labor, revolt, and flight]{claim=AMZ-C010}. Note the mechanism list: people did not only die in place. They were taken, gathered into missions, and they fled — most, the record says, from exposed locations along the major rivers. Nor did disease move as one wave: [in sparse lowlands epidemics commonly “faded out,” and it was the raids and the missions that kept reintroducing them]{claim=AMZ-C023}. A riverbank empty in 1690 is not evidence it was empty in 1542; it may be evidence of everything that happened in between.

The limit is that these counts come from upper-Amazon provinces with mission records. The Solimões reaches where the dispute actually lives have no equivalent reconstruction yet, and the reconciliation argument borrows ratios from where the records are.

## The sparse Amazon

Everything above could be true and the maximalist picture still false, and the negative evidence is part of this case's spine, not an afterthought. [Across 7,363 recorded archaeological sites, distance from a river is the single strongest predictor of pre-Columbian occupation, with the deep interfluves markedly sparser]{claim=AMZ-C013}. And [where scientists have cored the soils of the western and interfluvial Amazon — fourteen regions and counting — most terra-firme profiles show closed-canopy forest with little to no sign of crops, clearing, dark earths, tree enrichment, or recurrent fire]{claim=AMZ-C014}. The skeptics of the garden Amazon are not defending the old impossibility thesis; they are defending proportions — [predictive modeling over the known sites reckons the famous earthworks and dark earths cover a “limited, albeit impressive” fraction, with humbler site types dominating more than two-thirds of the basin]{claim=AMZ-C020} — and [the basin-wide earthwork model is reported to put almost 80 percent of Amazonia at a 0–1 percent chance of holding an earthwork in any given square kilometer, the low-probability country concentrated in the northwest, north, and center]{claim=AMZ-C029}, a figure this record has not yet verified against the paper's text and grades accordingly.

Both sides' sampling is biased, quantifiably. [The “sparse west” rests on some three hundred soil cores in five clusters — about a cubic meter of sediment standing in for two million square kilometers]{claim=AMZ-C021}, while [at Upano, forest recovery largely erased the pre-Columbian signal even though the later colonial signal survived, so a palaeoecological negative means less the older the activity]{claim=AMZ-C022}. And the site database that produces the river-distance gradient inherits the fact that archaeologists survey where they can reach. The case logs all of these biases rather than choosing one.

## What would decide it

Each live account makes a prediction the ledger can eventually check.

- **The corridor test.** Classify every reach of the 1541–42 route as populated or empty from the manuscripts alone, model the route's uncertainty, then compare contact-horizon (AD 1400–1650) archaeology in his populated reaches against matched controls. The murdered-world and mosaic readings predict a strong match; the modest skeptic predicts that his populated reaches are real but no denser than other bluff-and-channel settings; invention predicts nothing there at all.
- **The witness table.** A passage-by-passage collation of the manuscript branches. If the qualitative bedrock turns out to be branch-specific too, Carvajal's rehabilitation weakens; if only the figures are, it hardens.
- **Promise-blind surveys.** LiDAR and gridded coring across interfluvial blocks chosen without regard to archaeological promise, with controls for whether the method could have detected occupation. The garden Amazon predicts interfluve densities approaching riverine ones; the mosaic predicts a real but low matrix; the modest skeptic predicts near-zero outside a few hotspots.
- **Stratified LiDAR.** Survey blocks drawn at random within probability strata of the two earthwork models, to see which total is calibrated.
- **Dependency-corrected demography.** Sort every published estimate into its model family and re-derive them under one assumption set, so model families stop masquerading as independent censuses.
- **Middle-Amazon collapse timelines.** Extend province-by-province reconstruction to the Solimões, testing whether documented decline and relocation suffice to turn 1542 into the later silence.

## Where this case lands

[The pre-contact Amazon that survives every filter in this record is a strongly heterogeneous one: substantial populations, engineered subsistence, and settlement systems along favored corridors and hotspots, embedded in a much more lightly occupied forest matrix]{claim=AMZ-C016}. Neither the pristine wilderness nor the wall-to-wall civilization survives contact with the evidence; what remains open is proportions — and “heterogeneous” only earns its keep once the matrix density is measured rather than inferred.

How connected was this world? Here too the record splits along the line this case keeps drawing between what was found and what was inferred from it. [Regional interaction spheres are well documented — shared ceramic traditions, exchange, stable multilingualism; but the strong version, a continent-spanning Arawak-dominated integration, is assessed in the linguistic literature as resting on “quite weak” evidence]{claim=AMZ-C025}. The critic himself draws the boundary: doubting the continental network does not refute the regional spheres. That is the mosaic again, at the level of politics and language — real connection, bounded extent.

And the friar? [Carvajal now looks substantially credible about the qualitative social geography he described, and untrustworthy about his extreme numbers]{claim=AMZ-C017} — a more interesting vindication than the wholesale kind, because it is earned by discounting everything discountable and testing what is left. It is also provisional. The corroboration comes from the same corridors and the same genre of conquest narrative; the contact-horizon settlement systems dated so far lie downstream and to the south of his most famous passages; and the test that would close the question has not been run.

## Credit where the record supports it

One more genealogical fact belongs in the open. [Years before the 2026 results, Graham Hancock's *America Before* devoted seven chapters to the Amazonian discoveries — the Acre geoglyphs among them — and his 2024 series put Pärssinen and Ranzi themselves in front of a mass audience]{claim=AMZ-C018}, at a time when this research was marginal to the mainstream conversation. On this site, outsider status is not evidence — in either direction. Hancock's larger lost-civilization thesis is not what this evidence establishes, and the mainstream's numerical skepticism about Carvajal has been partly vindicated by the manuscript work. But a truthful genealogy records who kept the question alive while the instruments were catching up, and this is such a record.

assessment.synthesis: The thesis graded here is the heterogeneous one: substantial sedentary populations, engineered subsistence and settlement systems along favored corridors and hotspots, set in a much more lightly occupied forest matrix, with Carvajal qualitatively credible and numerically unreliable. It is carried from both directions. Positively: earthworks at enormous scale (AMZ-E001), fortified southern-rim villages dated AD 1250–1500 (AMZ-E004), settlement systems occupied into the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries at Santarém, Marajó and the Xingu (AMZ-E017, AMZ-E018, AMZ-E019), engineered year-round maize and fisheries where the carrying-capacity objection was strongest (AMZ-E014, AMZ-E022), and independent 1538 and 1560 witnesses converging on the same middle-Amazon reaches Carvajal described (AMZ-E007). Negatively: the river-distance gradient across 7,363 sites (AMZ-E010) and the thin intensive-use signal in fourteen sampled regions (AMZ-E011) cap the garden-Amazon reading, while the sampling critique (AMZ-C021) and time-graded erasure (AMZ-C022) keep those negatives from being read as proof of emptiness. Demography stays a set of assumption-driven envelopes (AMZ-E002, AMZ-E009), and the new basin-wide comparator (AMZ-E038, AMZ-E039) shows earthwork totals themselves differ several-fold between published models; the tree-species corroboration (AMZ-E040, AMZ-E041) is from one research network and counts once. Neither the invention reading nor the pristine wilderness survives the record; what the record cannot yet fix is the matrix density that separates the mosaic from the modest skeptic, and it cannot yet place contact-horizon archaeology on Carvajal's own reaches, since the dated systems lie downstream and to the south. Sensitivity: the single evidence record whose removal would most change the case verdict is AMZ-E007. Without it the Carvajal leg (AMZ-C017) drops to weakly supported, because every remaining corroboration is archaeological, off his route, or earlier than him, and the case verdict would fall to provisionally supported for the founding question even though the archaeological mosaic (AMZ-C016) would stand. On the matrix side, AMZ-E010 plays the equivalent role: without it the lightly occupied half rests on contested soil cores alone.
assessment.steelman: Every witness who saw the middle Amazon before the epidemics — Nunes in 1538, Carvajal in 1542, the ten Ursúa chroniclers in 1560 — reports the same specific, unglamorous features on the same reaches: stores of maize, long straight roads compared to Inca roads without walls, ceramics of known reputation, dense settlement. These witnesses wrote for different crowns, disliked one another, and did not copy one another; convergence on mundane detail is exactly what shared exaggeration does not produce. Nothing in the ledger contradicts them for those reaches — the negative evidence comes from interfluves and the west, not from the Solimões bluffs. Where colonial records permit counting, decline of 62–88 percent within a century and a half is documented, by mechanisms — flight from exposed river locations, gathering into missions, slave raids — that empty riverbanks specifically; every lower-Amazon settlement system dated so far runs to the seventeenth century and then stops; and the basin-wide radiocarbon proxy grows to the eve of contact with no endogenous crash. On this argument the burden lies on the skeptic to explain why corridor eyewitnesses should be discounted when nothing contradicts them where they stood, and this assessment has no record that does so; it holds Carvajal at provisionally supported only because the direct corridor test has not been run.
assessment.whatIsClaimed: That Gaspar de Carvajal's 1542 chronicle describes a real world — populous, organized, road-connected riverine societies along specific reaches of the Amazon; that Amazonian environments could and did support large sedentary populations with engineered subsistence, at scales revealed by LiDAR earthworks, dark earths, raised fields, canals and fish weirs; and that Old World epidemics, slave raiding, missionization and flight destroyed and dispersed that world fast enough that the emptier Amazon met by later travelers records a collapse rather than proving the earlier account false. The version this assessment grades is the heterogeneous one: dense corridors and hotspots embedded in a lightly occupied forest matrix, with Carvajal qualitatively credible and his extreme numbers a transmission artefact.
assessment.whereDisagreementLives: Not over whether complex Amazonian societies existed — earthworks, dark earths, engineered savannas and planned settlements are established beyond argument. The live cruxes are proportion and inference. How representative were the populated corridors of the basin, when river distance is the dominant predictor of known occupation and most sampled interfluves show little intensive modification — yet the negative sampling is thin and the pre-Columbian signal erodes with time? Do population estimates survive their own assumptions, when the largest recent figure falls roughly fivefold under the paper's own alternative reading, the field's most influential estimator rejected his own method, and earthwork totals differ several-fold between predictive models? How much of Carvajal is textual bedrock versus transmission artefact, when the most famous warrior counts sit in one manuscript branch only? And are spectacular but much earlier or geographically distant sites — the Aquiry peak of AD 100–300, the Casarabe world ending around 1400, the lower-Amazon systems — being silently spent as evidence about the reaches Carvajal saw in 1542?
assessment.whatWouldSettleIt: A preregistered Carvajal corridor test: classify his populated and empty reaches from the manuscript witnesses alone, model route and palaeochannel uncertainty, then compare contact-horizon archaeological intensity in his populated corridors against matched controls — before consulting the archaeological layers. Alongside it: a synoptic manuscript-witness table separating what every Carvajal branch shares from what one branch carries; promise-blind interfluve surveys with proxy-sensitivity controls to measure the matrix density directly; a probability-stratified, blind LiDAR sample to calibrate the competing earthwork totals; demographic estimates re-derived under a common assumption set; and province-by-province collapse timelines extended to the Solimões, so that the reconciliation argument stops borrowing ratios from provinces with records.
assessment.bestConventionalExplanation: The modern skeptical position is not the old ecological-impossibility argument; it concedes major regional societies and argues limits. Orellana travelled the richest corridors — the bluff-and-channel settings where settlement concentrated and where archaeology preferentially looks and preserves — so corroboration there cannot license basin-wide extrapolation. Sampled western and interfluvial palaeoecology shows large areas without intensive cultivation, clearing or soil modification, and predictive modeling over known sites finds the spectacular earthworks and dark earths a limited, if impressive, fraction. The famous population totals are model outputs whose assumptions — site contemporaneity, persons per earthwork, extrapolation domains — do most of the work, and the estimators themselves have said so. Carvajal's extreme figures are textually unstable across manuscript branches, consistent with a truthful observer whose numbers grew in the telling. On this view the mosaic is real but modest: dense hotspots, thin matrix, and a chronicle that is qualitatively honest and numerically unreliable, describing a world that was both smaller than legend and then genuinely destroyed.

components.label: Carvajal's qualitative social geography
components.note: Independent witnesses of 1538 and 1560 repeat the mundane load-bearing features on the same reaches (AMZ-E007); the bluff model makes his alternation of populated and empty stretches a testable spatial pattern (AMZ-E006). The corridor test that would close it (AMZ-R001) has not been run, and the dated contact-horizon systems lie off his most famous reaches.

components.label: Carvajal's extreme figures as counts
components.note: The 50,000, 10,000 and 8,000 warrior figures and the multi-league villages appear in the Medina/Muñoz branch and not in Oviedo (AMZ-E005); no witness independent of that branch carries them. The passage-level distribution across witnesses awaits the collation (AMZ-R002).

components.label: Earthworks, settlement systems and engineered subsistence
components.note: LiDAR, dating, phytoliths and zooarchaeology (AMZ-E001, AMZ-E004, AMZ-E014, AMZ-E017, AMZ-E018, AMZ-E022) put the ecological-impossibility thesis beyond rescue. The strongest cases are dated a millennium before Orellana or end before contact (AMZ-E003, AMZ-E014), and published earthwork totals differ several-fold between models (AMZ-E038, AMZ-E039).

components.label: Basin-wide demography
components.note: Estimates are model families sharing assumptions, not measurements: the Aquiry headline spans roughly fivefold under its own alternative (AMZ-E002), Denevan rejected his own method while keeping his order of magnitude (AMZ-E009), and the radiocarbon proxy shows growth without fixing scale (AMZ-E020). AMZ-R004 is the remedy.

components.label: Post-contact collapse as the reconciliation
components.note: Declines of 88 percent and 62–64 percent by 1700 are documented in upper-Amazon provinces by mixed mechanisms including flight from river locations (AMZ-E008); extension to the middle Amazon where the dispute lives is an extrapolation (AMZ-R005).

components.label: The lightly occupied matrix
components.note: River distance dominates occupation across 7,363 sites (AMZ-E010) and fourteen sampled regions show little intensive-use signal (AMZ-E011), but both records come from biased samples — survey effort toward rivers, roughly a cubic meter of cores for two million square kilometers, and time-graded erasure of the signal. The matrix density is inferred, not measured (AMZ-R003).

researchPriority.reason: The two most decisive tests — the Carvajal corridor test and the manuscript-witness table — are desk work on existing sources and would close or cap the founding question directly; the field items (promise-blind interfluve surveys, stratified LiDAR) are the only way to fix the matrix density and calibrate earthwork totals that currently differ several-fold. The evidence base is rich, recent and unusually well positioned for preregistered tests, and one ledger source is founder-funded, which makes independent calibration a matter of integrity as well as science.

claimAssessments.reasoning: This is a claim about what the chronicle says, and both anchoring sources (Denevan 1996 via AMZ-E006; Lopes et al. 2024 via AMZ-E007) confirm the described content, including the alternation of populated and empty stretches. The primary text has not been fetched natively; every statement about its content is mediated through scholars who quote and compare the branches, which is adequate for content but not for wording.

treatment.plainLanguage: Carvajal's chronicle really does describe crowded, organized riverbanks with roads, food stores and fine pottery — and also stretches with nobody.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishing what the text says decides nothing about whether it is true; its value is that the alternation of populated and empty reaches turns the account into a spatial prediction the bluff model (AMZ-E006) can test.
treatment.strongestObjection: Conquest-era chronicles were written for patrons with incentives to magnify; describing a world is not observing one, and the ledger reads the text only through two secondary comparisons.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A manuscript collation showing the qualitative description, not only the figures, differs between branches
Native reading of the primary text revealing content the secondary sources misreport

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E005 quotes Denevan's branch comparison verbatim: the 50,000, 10,000 and 8,000 warrior figures and the multi-league villages are in the Medina and Muñoz versions and absent from Oviedo, which carries one figure of about 5,000. Verification was via OCR full text. Which figure sits in which specific witness within the Medina/Muñoz family has not been re-read at page level; that is AMZ-R002's job and does not alter the branch-level finding.

treatment.plainLanguage: The giant numbers people quote from Carvajal appear in only one family of manuscripts; the other family describes the same crowded world without them.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Directly separates the numerical claims from the qualitative ones and licenses treating the latter as bedrock while refusing the former as counts — the hinge on which the whole Carvajal reading turns.
treatment.strongestObjection: Absence from Oviedo could reflect Oviedo's editing rather than Carvajal's original; the comparison rests on one scholar's reading verified from a scanned copy, and the assignment of each figure to each witness has not been independently re-read.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A page-level collation locating the 10,000 or 8,000 figures in Oviedo, or showing Oviedo systematically abridged numbers
Evidence that the qualitative descriptions also differ materially between branches

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E007 quotes Lopes et al. 2024 verbatim on Nunes's 1538 entry into Machiparo and the ten Ursúa accounts of 1560, with the specific shared features — dense habitation, infinite maize stores, wide straight roads compared to Inca roads without walls, turtle and fish in the thousands. The record's own limits are respected: fortifications and organized warfare are not among the shared elements, and the turtle-corral detail belongs to Acuña.

treatment.plainLanguage: Other Europeans who reached the same stretch of river before and after Carvajal, and who were not copying him, describe the same kind of crowded, road-connected world — without his giant numbers.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Independent convergence on mundane detail is the strongest available evidence for Carvajal's qualitative credibility and against the invention account; it is the single record whose removal would most weaken the case.
treatment.strongestObjection: All three traditions are conquest narratives sharing genre conventions and incentives; the Ursúa accounts were written eighteen years later and may have known Carvajal's; Nunes survives only as a letter of 1553/54 in a modern edition.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Evidence that the Ursúa chroniclers drew on Carvajal's text
A corridor test finding no contact-horizon settlement concentration on the Machiparo reaches

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E001 confirms verbatim the 432 earthworks from 10 laser lines, the 183,000 km² circumscription and the 24,000–30,000 projection as a block extrapolation. The claim states what the study documents and predicts, and that is established. AMZ-E038 and AMZ-E039 add context, not contradiction: a 2023 basin-wide model predicts 10,272–23,648 undiscovered earthworks for all Amazonia with its highest-probability cells in a 94,713 km² rectangle over Acre, so totals differ several-fold between models with different definitions and data. AMZ-E003 dates the Aquiry peak to AD 100–300.

treatment.plainLanguage: Laser survey found hundreds of hidden earthworks under the canopy in southwestern Amazonia and projects tens of thousands across the region — but the projection is an extrapolation, and a different model gives a much lower basin-wide number.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decisive against the ecological-impossibility account, but weak evidence about 1542: the florescence is a millennium earlier and the region is off Carvajal's route, and the several-fold spread between published totals means the scale itself is not yet calibrated.
treatment.strongestObjection: The 24,000–30,000 figure is a density extrapolation from sampled blocks that exceeds a basin-wide model's upper bound; the study is weeks old, unrebutted rather than accepted, and funded by this site's founder.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A blind, probability-stratified LiDAR sample (AMZ-R006) finding densities well below the regional projection
Redating that moves the Aquiry florescence toward or away from the contact horizon

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E002 quotes both the 1.25–3 million derivation (25–60 percent simultaneous use, 300 people per earthwork) and the single-family alternative of 250,000–600,000, or 315,000–760,000 with canopy correction, from the paper itself. The sensitivity is the authors' own; the emphasis on it is ours.

treatment.plainLanguage: The headline population for the ancient earthwork region depends on guesses about how many monuments were in use at once and how many people each took; change the guess and the number drops about fivefold.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides how the study's demography should be read — as an envelope, not a count — and stands as the template for the dependency audit of every published estimate.
treatment.strongestObjection: The authors label the single-family reading very unlikely; presenting the low end as an equal alternative may understate what house-mound size implies about household numbers.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Independent ethnoarchaeological or excavation evidence fixing persons per house foundation
Radiocarbon work fixing the simultaneous-use fraction empirically

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E004 quotes the 1,800 km occupation by fortified earth-building villages at cal AD 1250–1500 and the population derivation with its stated assumptions of contemporaneity, ethnographic formulae and MaxEnt projection. The occupation and dating are strongly supported; the 500,000–1,000,000 figure is a model and is graded as such within the claim.

treatment.plainLanguage: A vast arc along the southern edge of the Amazon was dotted with fortified villages in the two and a half centuries before Europeans arrived; the population attached to that is a model with named assumptions.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Contact-adjacent dating is what makes this diagnostic: it shows organized earth-building societies were present on the eve of contact, not only in antiquity — though on the southern rim, not Carvajal's river.
treatment.strongestObjection: The southern rim is far from the Solimões reaches Carvajal described, and the population range depends on every site being occupied at once.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Dating that shows widespread abandonment before 1500
Excavation showing the enclosures were not residential

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E014 quotes the drainage canals, savannah farm ponds, and phytolith analysis of 178 samples from 18 profiles recording the singular and ubiquitous presence of maize. The Casarabe florescence (500–1400 CE) ends before contact, which limits its bearing on 1542 but not its truth.

treatment.plainLanguage: In the Bolivian savannas one culture replumbed the landscape to grow maize year-round — canals for the floods, ponds for the dry season — and the maize is in the soil to prove it.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Directly answers the strongest old objection — that Amazonian environments could not feed sedentary populations — but a century and a half before Orellana and in savanna, not forest.
treatment.strongestObjection: Casarabe is a savanna society that ended around 1400; it says nothing about the forested riverbanks Carvajal saw or about their state in 1542.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Phytolith reanalysis showing maize confined to a few profiles rather than ubiquitous
Redating of the canal and pond systems

claimAssessments.reasoning: Dark earths, raised fields and forest islands are documented across the ledger (AMZ-E016, AMZ-E017, plates); the tree-domestication leg rests on AMZ-E012, corroborated by AMZ-E040 and AMZ-E041 with a different response variable but the same species list and overlapping authors, and qualified by AMZ-E013, which argues post-Columbian activity likely played the larger role in the modern floristic pattern. The landscape-engineering half is beyond dispute; the tree half is established as an association whose pre-Columbian share is contested.

treatment.plainLanguage: Humans reshaped Amazonian ground for centuries — fertile black soils, raised fields, artificial forest islands — and useful tree species cluster around old settlements, though how much of that clustering happened before 1492 is argued.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Establishes long engineering but not its extent or intensity; the tree signal cannot separate pre- from post-Columbian management, and its corroboration comes from one research network, so it does not raise the weight.
treatment.strongestObjection: Five post-Columbian centuries of land use may account for most of the modern domesticated-tree pattern, and the second study reuses the first's species list and authors.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Dated pre-Columbian tree-enrichment signals in cores away from known sites
An independent group with a different species list failing to reproduce the association

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E016 gives radiocarbon and OSL evidence of intermittent use from AD 570–770 in a few construction events linked to flood episodes, explicitly challenging the continuous-cultivation reading; AMZ-E015 supplies the flood-mitigation interpretation and the finding that fields were built only where there were no alternatives. Bermeo-area fields specifically.

treatment.plainLanguage: The famous raised fields were not a permanent breadbasket; they were built in a few bursts, probably when floods forced people's hands.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Cautions against reading engineering as continuous intensity — a check on the garden-Amazon inference from infrastructure to population.
treatment.strongestObjection: One field complex; other raised-field systems may have been cultivated continuously.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Dating of other complexes showing continuous multi-century use
Evidence of year-round cropping in raised-field soils

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E008 reproduces Newson's Table 1 figures — Napo-Aguarico 49,000–51,000 to 6,000 (87.8–88.2 percent), Mainas 62.3–63.6 percent — and the mixed mechanisms including revolt and flight from exposed river locations. The provinces are upper-Amazon with mission records; the baselines are themselves reconstructions.

treatment.plainLanguage: Where colonial records allow counting, populations fell by two-thirds to nearly nine-tenths within about 150 years — from disease, raids, missions, forced labor, revolt and flight, not disease alone.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Supplies the mechanism that reconciles a crowded 1542 with an empty 1690, and shows that emptying river banks specifically (flight, mission gathering) is documented — but for provinces upstream of the disputed reaches.
treatment.strongestObjection: Extension to the Solimões is an extrapolation; the pre-contact baselines are reconstructed, and a modest skeptic can accept these declines while holding that the middle-Amazon starting point was smaller than the chronicles imply.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Middle-Amazon mission records showing small populations at first sustained contact
Baseline re-estimates collapsing the early counts

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E017 (Belterra Plateau ca. AD 1300 to seventeenth-century colonization, with dark earths, ponds and trodden roads) and AMZ-E018 (Cacoal AD 1300–1650) are verbatim from primary reports; AMZ-E019 (Xingu 500–1770 CE, layouts matching Kuikuro villages) is journalism held at secondary weight pending the primary reports.

treatment.plainLanguage: Several large settlement systems were still inhabited when Europeans arrived, and one of them is continuous with villages people build today.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Contact-era occupation is the archaeology that overlaps Carvajal in time; it refutes invention and supports a murdered or diminished world — though at Santarém, Marajó and the Xingu, not on the Machiparo reaches.
treatment.strongestObjection: None of these systems lies on Carvajal's most famous reaches; their size in 1542 is not measured; the Xingu dates rest on a news feature.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Primary Xingu reports diverging from the summarized dates
Redating that ends Belterra or Cacoal occupation before contact

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E009 quotes Denevan rejecting the habitat-density method behind his 5.1–6.8 million estimate on grounds of within-habitat variability, while still believing at least 5 to 6 million reasonable. Graded decisive for the methodological point.

treatment.plainLanguage: The famous population totals are not independent measurements; the man behind the most-cited one has said the method that produced it does not work — while still believing the number.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Decides how every published total should be read and why the dependency audit (AMZ-R004) matters; it does not itself lower or raise the number.
treatment.strongestObjection: Denevan's self-criticism concerns method, not conclusion; convergence of several flawed methods on the same order of magnitude may still be informative.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: An independent method — settlement counts, dark-earth scaling — converging on a total under a common assumption set
A dependency audit showing the estimates are more independent than they look

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E010 quotes the 7,363-site model, river distance at 21.5 percent of permutation importance as the top predictor, and the finding that interfluvial areas were more sparsely populated than those near rivers. The site database inherits survey-effort bias toward accessible riverine areas, which the source acknowledges as a limitation.

treatment.plainLanguage: Across thousands of known sites, being near a river is the best predictor of ancient occupation; the deep forest between rivers was much emptier.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The main quantitative support for the lightly occupied matrix and against the garden Amazon; also consistent with the bluff model that makes Carvajal's alternation of full and empty reaches expected.
treatment.strongestObjection: Archaeologists survey where they can reach, which is along rivers; interfluvial sites such as Loma Salvatierra exist, and the gradient may partly measure survey effort.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Promise-blind interfluve surveys (AMZ-R003) finding occupation densities comparable to riverine ones
Bias-corrected models flattening the river-distance effect

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E011 quotes the cumulative synthesis: little to no evidence for annual crops, significant clearing, anthropic soils, tree enrichment or recurrent fire in most sampled terra-firme settings. New fieldwork covers three regions; fourteen is cumulative. The sampling critique (AMZ-C021) and time-graded erasure (AMZ-C022) limit how far the negative can be pushed.

treatment.plainLanguage: Where scientists have cored the soils of the western and interfluvial Amazon, most show old forest with little sign of farming, clearing or fire before Columbus.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: The palaeoecological leg of the matrix argument; strongly against the garden Amazon where sampled, but its reach depends on how representative roughly a cubic meter of cores is and how much older signal has eroded.
treatment.strongestObjection: Three hundred cores in five clusters standing for two million square kilometers, and forest recovery demonstrably erases pre-Columbian signals while preserving colonial ones.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Denser gridded coring with sensitivity controls detecting intensive-use signals in interfluves
Demonstration that the proxies systematically miss pre-Columbian activity of the relevant age

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E020 quotes the logistic fit over 1,700 years and the authors' attribution of the terminal decline to sampling bias compounded by post-contact collapse. Summed radiocarbon distributions are proxies for relative change with stated biases; the only record for this claim is moderate strength.

treatment.plainLanguage: Pooled radiocarbon dates suggest Amazonian populations were still growing, or had leveled off, right up to European arrival — not already declining.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Rules against a pre-European endogenous crash as an alternative to collapse, which helps the murdered-world reading, but fixes nothing about scale — carrying capacity, however high, is not a number.
treatment.strongestObjection: Summed probability distributions are shaped by which sites archaeologists date; the terminal dip could be read either way, and the authors' attribution of it to bias plus collapse is an interpretation.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Bias-corrected date distributions showing pre-contact decline
Regional records of abandonment before 1500 across multiple basins

claimAssessments.reasoning: The synthesis rests on both legs being carried: hotspots by AMZ-E001, AMZ-E004, AMZ-E014, AMZ-E017, AMZ-E018, AMZ-E022; matrix by AMZ-E010 and AMZ-E011. The heterogeneous reading is what survives both the positive and negative records. Its open parameter — the matrix density — is inferred from biased samples on both sides, which is why confidence is moderate rather than high.

treatment.plainLanguage: On the eve of contact the Amazon was neither empty wilderness nor wall-to-wall civilization: crowded, engineered corridors and hotspots set in much emptier forest.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the thesis; its diagnosticity against the modest skeptic and the garden Amazon depends on a matrix-density measurement that does not yet exist, so it is presently a framing both can partly inhabit.
treatment.strongestObjection: Heterogeneous can absorb almost any finding; without a measured matrix density it is not falsifiable, and the negative record it rests on is as biased as the positive one.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Promise-blind surveys giving interfluve densities approaching riverine ones (toward the garden Amazon)
Promise-blind surveys giving near-zero densities everywhere outside a few hotspots (toward the modest skeptic)

claimAssessments.reasoning: Depends on AMZ-C001, AMZ-C002 and AMZ-C003 (the numbers are branch-specific; independent witnesses repeat the qualitative world) plus AMZ-C006 and AMZ-C011 for contact-era archaeology. AMZ-E003 qualifies: the most spectacular earthworks are a millennium too early to bear on 1542. The dated settlement systems lie off his most famous reaches and the corridor test has not been run, so the rehabilitation is provisional.

treatment.plainLanguage: Carvajal probably told the truth about the kind of world he saw, and probably not about how many warriors were in it.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: This is the answer to the founding question in its current state; it decides between invention and the live accounts, but not among the live accounts, which differ over scale rather than credibility.
treatment.strongestObjection: Every corroboration is either the same genre of conquest narrative on the same corridors, or archaeology dated earlier or located elsewhere; no contact-horizon archaeology has yet been compared reach by reach against his populated and empty stretches, and the route itself is uncertain.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: A null result in the preregistered corridor test (AMZ-R001)
A collation showing the qualitative descriptions are also branch-specific
Evidence that the Ursúa chroniclers depended on Carvajal's text

claimAssessments.reasoning: Hancock's first-party statement of seven chapters and more than 90 pages is quoted from his site; AMZ-E021 documents Pärssinen and Ranzi in the S2.E1 cast listing. The book itself is unverified background. The record explicitly carries no weight for any empirical claim about the Amazon.

treatment.plainLanguage: A popular author gave the Amazonian earthworks a mass audience years before the big LiDAR result, and put the researchers on screen.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Genealogy, not evidence: it decides nothing about the Amazon in either direction and is recorded so the credit trail is honest.
treatment.strongestObjection: A cast listing and a self-description establish coverage, not influence on the research; and the lost-civilization thesis the coverage served is not what the evidence supports.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Page-level verification of the book's Amazon chapters contradicting the self-description
Evidence the chapters misrepresented the research they popularized

claimAssessments.reasoning: Rests on a verified source anchor quoting the authors' postulate that the V-shaped structures concentrated fish in ponds, with the 382 ponds and proximity finding recorded in the source verification; no separate evidence record carries it, and the source itself notes the structures concentrate fish far less intensely than modern analogues.

treatment.plainLanguage: People built miles of zigzag weirs and causeways across the Bolivian floodplains, with ponds beside them, to trap fish as the floods drained.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Adds an engineered protein source to the answer against the impossibility account and softens the strict river-distance reading of the matrix; the function is the authors' inference from form and layout.
treatment.strongestObjection: Function is inferred, not observed; the weirs concentrate fish weakly compared to modern analogues; and the system is savanna, not forest.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Experimental or zooarchaeological evidence that the weirs did not function as fish traps
Dating that separates the weirs from the settlement systems they are assumed to have fed

claimAssessments.reasoning: AMZ-E022 quotes more than 17,000 fish remains at Loma Salvatierra, 50 km from the Mamoré, occupied 500–1400 AD, demonstrating year-round interfluvial aquatic resources with lungfish and tiger-fish among the dry-season species. One site, and the source itself notes the paucity of large river fish.

treatment.plainLanguage: Bones from one mound fifty kilometers from the big river show people fishing local waters all year, including the dry season.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: An existence proof that interfluves could feed sedentary people through the year, which the old skepticism denied; it is one site and not a census.
treatment.strongestObjection: A single site in a managed savanna cannot stand for interfluvial forest, and the occupation ends before contact.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Reanalysis showing the assemblage is seasonal rather than year-round
Comparable interfluvial sites with no such record

claimAssessments.reasoning: Rests on a verified source anchor (Walker et al. 2023) quoting the limited, albeit impressive, predicted extents of earthworks and dark earths and other sites dominating more than two-thirds of Amazonia; no separate evidence record carries it. The model is built from the same biased site base as AMZ-C013.

treatment.plainLanguage: Machine-learning maps of where sites should be say the famous earthworks and black soils cover a limited share of the basin, with humbler kinds of site elsewhere.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: States the modest skeptic's proportions claim in quantitative form; it does not say the rest was empty, only that it was different, so it is compatible with both the mosaic and the modest skeptic.
treatment.strongestObjection: Predictions over known sites reproduce discovery bias; the two-thirds is a modelled dominance of site types, not a measured density.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Blind surveys finding earthworks or dark earths common in areas the model assigns to other site types
A separate evidence record verifying the quoted proportions in the text

claimAssessments.reasoning: Rests on a verified source anchor (the Clement et al. reply) quoting roughly 300 cores in five small areas totaling 1.17 m³ to represent 2,000,000 km² of western Amazonia; no separate evidence record. It is a critique of sampling density, not a positive finding of occupation.

treatment.plainLanguage: The soil evidence for a sparse western Amazon comes from about a cubic meter of sediment drawn from five spots in an area the size of Mexico.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Limits how far the negative palaeoecological record can be pushed against the garden Amazon; it weakens the modest skeptic's strongest leg without adding any positive evidence of occupation.
treatment.strongestObjection: Sparse sampling cuts both ways — it also cannot show occupation — and the sampled regions were chosen where occupation might have been expected.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Denser, gridded coring programs in the same regions confirming the negative
Demonstration that the existing cores are statistically representative

claimAssessments.reasoning: Rests on a verified source anchor (Bush et al. 2025) quoting that a long period of forest recovery largely eradicated the influence of pre-Columbian occupations, with the colonial-period signal persisting; no separate evidence record. One valley, the Upano, where urbanism is independently documented.

treatment.plainLanguage: In one valley known to have held ancient towns, the forest grew back so completely that the soil record barely shows them — while later colonial activity still shows.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Shows that a negative palaeoecological result means less the older the activity, which reduces the weight of the sparse-west record for the pre-Columbian era specifically.
treatment.strongestObjection: One valley with a particular recovery history; erasure rates elsewhere are not measured, and the argument risks making the negative record unfalsifiable.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Paired studies elsewhere showing pre-Columbian signals persist where occupation is independently known
Proxy calibration giving detection thresholds by age

claimAssessments.reasoning: Rests on Newson 2003 (the source of AMZ-E008), whose mixed-mechanism passages — epidemics, enslaving raids, missionization, unrest — support the interactive reading; the fading-out formulation is anchored to the source but not carried by a separate evidence record.

treatment.plainLanguage: In thinly settled lowlands epidemics often burned out rather than sweeping everyone; it was raids and mission gathering that kept bringing disease back.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: Explains why collapse could be uneven and prolonged, which matters for reconciling a populated 1542 with later silence, and why a single early pandemic is not the required mechanism.
treatment.strongestObjection: Documented for upper-Amazon provinces with mission records; the middle Amazon's disease history is inferred.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Middle-Amazon documentary evidence of a single sweeping early epidemic
Province-level timelines (AMZ-R005) contradicting the interactive pattern

claimAssessments.reasoning: The claim states a specific proportion — almost 80 percent of Amazonia at 0–1 percent earthwork probability per km² cell, concentrated in the northwest, north and center — attributed to the 2023 basin-wide model. The evidence record intended to anchor it failed verification because the quoted span was not found verbatim in the open-access text, and no other ledger record carries the figure. The source is in the ledger (AMZ-E038, AMZ-E039) and the proportion is plausible given its high-probability rectangle, but plausibility is a prior, not evidence.

treatment.plainLanguage: The basin-wide model is said to leave almost four-fifths of the Amazon with essentially no predicted earthworks — a figure this record has not yet confirmed in the paper.
treatment.diagnosticitySummary: If verified it is the sparse account's most quotable number and the target of the stratified LiDAR test; unverified, it decides nothing and is featured because of its stakes, not its support.
treatment.strongestObjection: The figure has not been located in the paper's text; and even if correct, a modelled probability surface trained on biased discovery data is a prediction to be tested, not a measurement of emptiness.
whatWouldChangeOurMind: Page-level verification of the percentage in the paper or its supplement
Blind LiDAR blocks in the 0–1 percent stratum (AMZ-R006) finding earthworks at appreciable density
